guides.title: Explain concepts related to system and network architecture in security operations
guides.core: Security operations only works if telemetry is trustworthy and complete. Architecture decisions (where logs come from, how networks are segmented, how identities are verified) decide what an analyst can see and what an attacker can reach.
know: Log ingestion pipeline: generate, collect, normalize, enrich, store, correlate. Time sync (NTP) is a prerequisite for correlation.
Windows and Linux artifacts that matter: registry run keys, services, scheduled tasks, auth logs, configuration files, process trees.
Virtualization, containers and serverless change what you can monitor: ephemeral workloads need centralized logging and image controls.
Segmentation limits lateral movement; zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location and verifies every request.
Identity: MFA, SSO, federation, privileged access management, passwordless. Encryption: PKI, TLS inspection trade-offs, data-at-rest protection.
guides.decide: When a design question asks how to reduce blast radius, choose segmentation or least privilege. When it asks how to trust events, choose time sync and centralized, tamper-resistant logging.
traps: More log volume is not better visibility: unsynchronized or unparsed logs cannot be correlated.
TLS inspection improves visibility but adds privacy, performance and key-management risk.

deep.title: Infrastructure models and where visibility goes
points: Virtualization: a hypervisor shares hardware between full guest operating systems. Watch for snapshot sprawl, unpatched templates and hypervisor access.
Containers share the host kernel and are built from images. Control image provenance, scan images, and use runtime isolation; send logs off the container because it is short-lived.
Serverless: the provider runs servers and the operating system, you own function code, permissions and data. Monitor through provider logs and keep each function's role least-privilege.
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud itself; you secure what you configure and store in it. Misconfiguration is your risk in every model.

deep.title: Operating system and device concepts to recognize
points: Windows persistence and evidence: registry Run keys (HKCU and HKLM), services, scheduled tasks, and Security event log entries such as 4624 (logon), 4625 (failed logon) and 4672 (special privileges).
Linux: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, authentication logs (auth.log or secure), cron jobs, systemd units and configuration files under /etc.
Hardening: remove unused services, apply least privilege, patch, and apply a baseline such as CIS. Hardware roots of trust include TPM, secure boot and HSMs.
Device management: MDM or UEM enforces configuration, can separate work data from personal data, and supports selective or full remote wipe.

deep.title: Critical infrastructure and data protection
points: OT and ICS (SCADA, PLCs) prioritize availability and safety first. The Purdue model layers field devices up to the enterprise network; keep OT segmented from IT and use passive monitoring.
When a legacy OT device cannot be patched, use compensating controls: segmentation, allow-listing, strict access and monitoring.
Data protection: classify data, then use encryption at rest and in transit, DLP, tokenization (replace with a surrogate), masking (hide part of the value) and key management through PKI or an HSM.
TLS inspection restores visibility into encrypted traffic but adds privacy, performance and key-handling risk.

guides.title: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of potential malicious activity
guides.core: Indicators are clues, not verdicts. The skill is to recognize an abnormal pattern, then decide which additional evidence confirms or refutes malicious intent.
know: Network: beaconing at regular intervals, unusual outbound volume, scans and sweeps, traffic on unexpected ports, rogue devices.
Host: unexpected processes, new scheduled tasks or services, registry or file changes, privilege changes, resource spikes.
Application: new accounts, unexpected outbound connections, unusual output or errors, service interruptions.
Social engineering and obfuscated links: check sender alignment, URL destination and attachment behavior.
guides.decide: Rank an indicator by how specific it is and what corroborates it. A single odd event triggers investigation; several independent indicators justify containment.
traps: Assuming one indicator proves compromise. Business activity (a VPN, a patch window, a backup job) explains many anomalies.
Ignoring slow, low-volume activity because it does not spike a threshold.

deep.title: Indicators by location
points: Network: beaconing at regular intervals with small, similar requests; unusual outbound volume; scans and sweeps; traffic on unexpected ports; rogue devices; DNS tunneling (long random subdomains, many TXT queries).

Host: abnormal parent-child processes (a document spawning PowerShell), new scheduled tasks or services, registry Run key changes, unauthorized software, privilege changes, and high CPU, memory or disk use.
Application: new accounts, unexpected output or errors, unexpected outbound connections and service interruptions.
Cloud: unusual API calls, new access keys, IAM policy changes, disabled logging, public storage buckets and activity from unfamiliar regions.

deep.title: Email attacks and living off the land
points: Business email compromise impersonates an executive or vendor to redirect payments. Tells: urgency, new bank details, mismatched Reply-To, lookalike domains.
Check SPF (sending server authorized), DKIM (message signed) and DMARC (policy plus alignment with the visible From domain). Read the Received headers from the bottom up.
Obfuscated links use shorteners, lookalike characters or redirects. Inspect the real destination before clicking.

Living off the land abuses legitimate tools such as PowerShell, WMI, certutil, bitsadmin, rundll32, mshta and PsExec. Detect through unusual command lines, parent processes and rarity, not file hashes.

guides.title: Given a scenario, use tools to determine malicious activity
guides.core: Tools collect evidence; techniques turn it into a conclusion. Know what question each tool answers and what it cannot see.
know: Packet analysis (Wireshark, tcpdump) shows what crossed the wire; EDR shows host behavior; SIEM correlates across sources; IDS/IPS match signatures or anomalies.
File and email analysis: hashing, strings, sandboxing, header review, SPF, DKIM and DMARC alignment.
Lookups (WHOIS, dig, nslookup) give context about domains and addresses, not intent.
Scripting literacy: read regex, JSON, SQL, PowerShell, Python and Bash well enough to interpret what a command or log query does.
guides.decide: Match the tool to the evidence source: network question, packet or flow data; endpoint question, EDR or memory; cross-system question, SIEM.
traps: A clean hash lookup does not prove a file is safe; novel malware has no reputation yet.
Encrypted traffic limits payload inspection; use metadata, certificates and behavior.

deep.title: Decoding and parsing
points: Base64 uses A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /, often ends with =, and is encoding, not encryption. PowerShell -EncodedCommand expects Base64 of UTF-16LE text.
URL encoding replaces characters with %XX (%20 space, %27 single quote, %3C less-than). Decode before judging a web request.
Hex, ROT13 and single-byte XOR are common lightweight obfuscations. CyberChef or command-line tools decode them; always do it in a safe environment.
Parse logs with grep, awk, cut, sort and uniq -c, jq for JSON, and regular expressions for patterns.

deep.title: WHOIS, DNS lookups and scripting languages
points: WHOIS shows registrar, registration and expiry dates and registrant details. A domain registered days ago with hidden registrant details is more suspicious.
dig and nslookup query DNS: A and AAAA (addresses), MX (mail), NS (name servers), TXT (text, SPF), CNAME (alias), PTR (reverse lookup, dig -x).

Read regex: . any character, * zero or more, + one or more, ? optional, ^ start, $ end, [ ] character set, \d digit, \w word character, { } counts. Read JSON (key/value pairs, arrays in [ ]) and XML (nested tags).

Recognize SQL injection (' OR 1=1--, UNION SELECT), PowerShell (Verb-Noun cmdlets, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, IEX, DownloadString), Python (import socket, subprocess) and Bash (pipes, redirects, curl piped into sh).

deep.title: Suspicious command patterns
points: Download and run: certutil -urlcache -f, bitsadmin /transfer, curl or wget piped to a shell, PowerShell DownloadString with IEX.
Proxy execution: mshta with a URL, regsvr32 with /i:http, rundll32 with javascript:, wmic process call create.
Persistence and privilege: schtasks /create, net user /add, net localgroup administrators /add, new services.
Impact: vssadmin delete shadows (removes recovery points before ransomware), wevtutil cl (clears logs), netcat with -e (reverse shell).

guides.title: Explain threat intelligence and threat-hunting concepts
guides.core: Threat intelligence is only useful when it is relevant, timely and graded for reliability. Hunting is hypothesis-driven: assume a technique is in use and look for its evidence.
know: Actor types: nation-state, organized crime, hacktivist, insider, unskilled attacker. Motivation shapes targeting.
Indicators of compromise (IPs, hashes, domains) are cheap for attackers to change; behaviors (TTPs) are costly to change and better for detection.
Admiralty scale: source reliability A to F and information credibility 1 to 6, rated independently.
Sharing: ISACs, OSINT, commercial feeds. Hunts start from a hypothesis, an intel report or an anomaly.
guides.decide: Prefer detections built on behavior over single IPs or hashes, and prefer intelligence you can tie to your sector and technology stack.
traps: Treating all feed entries as equally trustworthy or current.
Confusing a hunt with alert triage: hunting begins without an alert.

deep.title: Pyramid of Pain and intelligence quality
points: Pyramid of Pain from easiest to hardest for the attacker to change: hash values, IP addresses, domain names, network and host artifacts, tools, then TTPs. Detecting higher levels costs the attacker more.
Rate sources and information separately (Admiralty). Confidence changes the action: high confidence can drive blocking, low confidence belongs in monitoring and hunting until corroborated.
Intelligence levels: strategic (leadership and trends), operational (campaigns and actor intent), tactical (TTPs and indicators for defenders).
Timeliness, relevance and accuracy decide usefulness. Stale indicators generate noise.

deep.title: Collection sources, STRIDE and hunting
points: Sources: OSINT, commercial and open feeds, ISACs and ISAOs for peer sharing, dark web monitoring, honeypots and honeynets, internal telemetry and vulnerability feeds.
STRIDE threat model: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Use it at design time to find threats.
Threat actors: nation-state (long-term, stealthy, resourced), organized crime (profit), hacktivist (ideology), insider (access and grievance), unskilled attackers (tools others built).
Hunting starts from a hypothesis tied to intelligence or an ATT&CK technique, searches telemetry, and ends with a new detection, a fix or a documented negative result.

guides.title: Explain the importance of efficiency and process improvement in security operations
guides.core: Efficiency means removing repeatable manual work and inconsistent decisions so analysts spend time on judgment.
know: Standardize with runbooks and playbooks; automate with SOAR, scripts, APIs and webhooks.
Automate enrichment and low-risk containment first; keep humans approving high-impact actions.
Measure improvement: time to triage, false-positive rate, case backlog, analyst time per ticket.
guides.decide: Automate tasks that are high-volume, well understood and reversible. Keep a human in the loop where a mistake causes an outage or destroys evidence.
traps: Automating a bad process just makes errors faster.
Treating a lower alert count as improvement without checking that detection coverage held.

deep.title: Playbooks, tuning and automation building blocks
points: A playbook guides response to an incident type (roles, decisions, escalation). A runbook gives step-by-step technical instructions for a task and is a good automation candidate.
Tune rules with narrow, documented exclusions, thresholds and added context. Re-measure precision and missed detections after each change; never suppress blindly.
Automation parts: APIs (request and response), webhooks (push an event when something happens), plugins and connectors, and SOAR to orchestrate several tools.
Infrastructure as code and CI/CD make configuration versioned, reviewable and repeatable. Standardize handoffs with ticketing and shift handover notes.

guides.title: Summarize concepts related to the use of AI in security operations
guides.core: AI in security operations speeds triage and drafting but introduces new failure modes: fabricated output, manipulated input, data leakage and drifting accuracy.
know: Useful applications: summarization, alert enrichment, anomaly detection, script drafting, report writing.
Risks: hallucination, bias, prompt injection (including indirect injection through untrusted content), training-data poisoning, leakage of sensitive data into external services.
Controls: human review of consequential actions, least-privilege tool access, approved enterprise tools, logging of prompts and outputs, data classification rules, monitoring for drift.
guides.decide: Treat AI output as an unverified draft. Verify before acting; limit what an AI agent can do without approval.
traps: Assuming a confident answer is a correct answer.
Pasting sensitive data into an unapproved external model.

deep.title: AI use cases and usage policies
points: Good fits: summarizing timelines and alerts, drafting reports, enrichment, anomaly detection, phishing triage and script drafting, all with human verification.

A usage policy covers approved tools, what data may be entered (classification limits), required human review, logging of prompts and outputs, vendor data-retention terms and periodic accuracy and bias testing.
Risks to name: hallucination, bias, prompt injection, data poisoning, model inversion and leakage of sensitive data to third parties.
Do not let an AI agent take high-impact actions without approval and rollback.

guides.title: Given a scenario, implement the appropriate vulnerability scanning method
guides.core: Scan design is a set of trade-offs between depth, safety and coverage. Choose the method that fits the asset and the question.
know: Credentialed scans see patch levels and local configuration; non-credentialed scans show what an outsider can see.
Agent-based scanning covers roaming or isolated devices; agentless needs network reach.
Active scanning probes; passive scanning observes traffic and is gentler on fragile systems such as OT and ICS.
Plan scope, schedule and impact: maintenance windows, sensitivity of assets, segmentation and regulatory needs.
guides.decide: For fragile or safety-critical systems prefer passive or carefully tuned scanning coordinated with operations. For accuracy on managed hosts prefer credentialed scans.
traps: Running aggressive scans against production OT or legacy devices without coordination.
Treating an unauthenticated scan result as a complete patch inventory.

deep.title: Planning scans and choosing a method
points: Plan scope from the asset inventory, schedule within maintenance windows, tune intensity to limit performance impact, and allow scanner traffic through segmentation and firewalls.
Credentialed scans see installed software and configuration (fewer false positives); non-credentialed scans show the outside view.
Agent-based scanning covers roaming devices; agentless needs network reach. Active scans probe; passive scans observe traffic and are safer for fragile systems.
Internal scans find lateral exposure; external scans show what the internet can reach. SAST reads source code without running it; DAST tests the running application.

deep.title: Frameworks behind scanning requirements
points: PCI DSS governs payment card environments (including regular internal and external scans). CIS Benchmarks give prescriptive hardening settings.
OWASP supplies web application guidance (Top 10, ASVS, testing guide). ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 define an information security management system and controls.
Compliance scanning compares configuration against a baseline; vulnerability scanning looks for known flaws. They answer different questions.

guides.title: Given a scenario, analyze output from vulnerability assessment tools
guides.core: Scanner output is a lead list. Validate findings, understand what the score does and does not say, and separate true from false positives.
know: False positive: reported but not real. False negative: real but not reported. Validate by credentialed check, version confirmation or safe proof.
CVSS v4.0 groups: Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental. Exploit maturity is a Threat metric. A partial vector cannot give a complete score.
Nmap states: open, closed, filtered (probes blocked, state unknown), open|filtered.
Interpret tool output (Nessus, OpenVAS, Burp, ZAP, Nmap) in context of asset and exposure.
guides.decide: Never suppress or accept a finding on gut feeling; verify it against an independent source and record the reasoning.
traps: Equating a high CVSS base score with high risk in your environment.
Reading filtered as closed.

deep.title: Tools and reading their output
points: Scanners: Nessus, OpenVAS and Qualys find known vulnerabilities. Nmap discovers hosts, ports and versions. Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP are intercepting proxies for web applications. Metasploit validates exploitability.
A finding normally shows severity, CVE or plugin ID, affected asset, evidence (such as a banner), and a recommended fix. Banner-only evidence can be wrong when vendors backport fixes.

True positive: reported and real. False positive: reported but not real. True negative: not reported and not present. False negative: not reported but present (often caused by missing access or credentials).
Validate with an independent method and record the result.

guides.title: Given a scenario, analyze data to prioritize and mitigate vulnerabilities
guides.core: Prioritization combines severity, likelihood and business impact. Severity scores alone mislead.
know: Severity (CVSS), likelihood of exploitation (EPSS, which estimates probability of exploitation activity over the next 30 days), evidence of exploitation (CISA KEV), exposure (internet-facing or internal), asset criticality.
Mitigation options: patch, configuration change, compensating controls such as segmentation, virtual patching or restricted access, and monitoring while a fix is staged.
Weakness classes to recognize: injection, XSS, CSRF, broken access control, insecure deserialization.
guides.decide: Rank first by known exploitation and exposure on critical assets, then by severity. If you cannot patch now, reduce exposure and document the exception with an owner and end date.
traps: Patching strictly in CVSS order and missing a medium-score flaw that is actively exploited.
Using an exception as permanent risk acceptance without approval.

deep.title: Prioritization inputs and secure coding
points: Combine CVSS severity, EPSS likelihood, CISA KEV (known exploitation), exploit availability, asset criticality, exposure, patch availability and compensating controls.
A zero-day has no vendor fix when attackers start using it, so isolate, disable the vulnerable feature, virtually patch and monitor.

Secure coding: validate input against an allow-list, use parameterized queries (stops SQL injection), encode output for the context (stops XSS), apply least privilege, manage secrets and dependencies, and test with SAST and DAST.
Fix the cause, not only the symptom: sanitizing one parameter does not remove a missing-access-control flaw.

guides.title: Explain concepts related to control types, risks, and vulnerability management
guides.core: Controls and risk decisions give vulnerability work a business frame: what reduces risk, how, and who accepts what remains.
know: Control functions: preventive, detective, corrective, compensating. Categories: managerial, operational, technical.
Risk responses: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept. Acceptance needs a documented owner.
Patch management depends on change control, testing, maintenance windows and SLAs.
guides.decide: Identify what the control does (stops, finds, fixes or substitutes) before naming its type.
traps: Calling a compensating control a permanent fix.
Confusing avoid (stop the activity) with mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact).

deep.title: Supply chain, exceptions and control types
points: Supply chain risk comes from vendors, libraries and build pipelines. Keep a software bill of materials (SBOM), verify signatures and integrity, and assess suppliers.
Control functions: preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, and deterrent. A compensating control stands in when the preferred control is impractical.
A remediation exception needs a business reason, an accountable owner, compensating controls and an expiry or review date.

guides.title: Summarize concepts related to attack methodology frameworks
guides.core: Attack frameworks give analysts a shared vocabulary for describing intrusions and finding gaps in detection.
know: Cyber Kill Chain: a linear model of stages from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.
Diamond Model: adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim as core features, pivoted to link events.
MITRE ATT&CK: tactics (the goal) and techniques (the method), used to map observed behavior and plan detection coverage.
OSSTMM and the OWASP testing guide describe testing methodology.
guides.decide: Use ATT&CK to label behavior and measure detection coverage, the Kill Chain to reason about where to break an attack, and the Diamond Model to relate events and actors.
traps: Treating the Kill Chain as the only sequence real attackers follow.
Mixing up a tactic (why) with a technique (how).

deep.title: Kill Chain, Diamond Model and ATT&CK compared
points: Cyber Kill Chain stages in order: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives. Breaking any link stops the attack; defenders map controls to each stage.

Diamond Model: every event has an adversary, a capability, infrastructure and a victim. Analysts pivot between features (the same infrastructure used against two victims) to link events and campaigns.

MITRE ATT&CK catalogs real-world behavior. A tactic is the adversary's goal in a phase (persistence, lateral movement); a technique is how it is achieved (scheduled task, pass-the-hash). Use it to label what you saw and to find detection gaps.
OSSTMM is a methodology for testing operational security across channels. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is the methodology for testing web applications.

guides.title: Summarize the incident response process
guides.core: An incident response process turns confusion into ordered work. Each stage has a different goal and exit condition.
know: Stages used by this objective: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, post-incident activity.
Other models group these differently (for example NIST combines containment, eradication and recovery). Keep model names labeled when comparing.
Preparation covers plans, tools, training and contacts. Post-incident work includes lessons learned and updating detection and playbooks.
guides.decide: Decide which stage you are in from the goal: understand (analysis), stop spread (containment), remove cause (eradication), restore service (recovery), improve (post-incident).
traps: Eradicating before scoping the incident, which lets the attacker return.
Skipping lessons learned once service is restored.

deep.title: Incident response stages and what belongs in each
points: Preparation: plan, roles, tools, training and exercises done before anything happens. Detection and analysis: confirm the incident, scope it, and classify severity.
Containment limits spread and damage (short term: isolate; long term: segment, rebuild plans). Eradication removes the cause: malware, persistence, vulnerable component, compromised credentials.

Recovery restores service from known-good sources, validates function, and monitors for recurrence. Post-incident activity captures lessons learned, updates detections and playbooks, and finalizes reporting.

Tabletop exercises test decisions without touching systems. Severity classification drives escalation, staffing and notification. The incident commander coordinates and holds authority during the response.

guides.title: Given a scenario, implement incident response techniques
guides.core: Response techniques have to contain harm while preserving evidence and meeting legal obligations.
know: Order of volatility: capture memory and running state before disk and archived data.
Forensic integrity: write blockers, cryptographic hashes of source and image, documented chain of custody.
Containment options: network isolation, account disablement, segmentation, blocking indicators. Isolation usually beats power-off when memory matters.
Legal hold suspends deletion of relevant records. Communicate on a need-to-know basis.
guides.decide: Contain quickly, but pick containment that keeps volatile evidence and does not destroy options for later analysis.
traps: Wiping and reimaging before capturing evidence.
Letting automatic log deletion continue under a legal hold.

deep.title: Enrichment, timelines and isolation
points: Enrich events with asset owner and criticality, user identity, geolocation and reputation so triage is faster and more accurate.
Build timelines from several sources after normalizing timestamps to one time zone (UTC) and checking clock accuracy.
Isolate with EDR network containment, a quarantine VLAN or blocking at the switch. These keep the system and its memory intact and let responders reach it.
Release a host only after eradication, validation (or rebuild from a known-good image), credential resets and monitoring are in place.

deep.title: Eradication, recovery and corrective action
points: Eradicate by removing malware and persistence, closing the entry point and resetting credentials. Rebuild from known-good media when integrity is in doubt.
Recover by restoring from verified backups, validating function, and watching closely for reinfection.
Corrective actions address the root cause: patching, configuration changes, new detections, training and process updates, each with an owner and date.

guides.title: Explain the importance of vulnerability management reporting and communication
guides.core: Vulnerability reporting must let different audiences make decisions. A report that cannot drive action has failed.
know: Contents: scope, method, findings prioritized by risk, affected assets, owners, recommended action, exceptions and trends.
Audience: executives need risk and business impact; engineers need exact steps and evidence.
Track remediation: time to remediate by severity, SLA compliance, recurring findings, aging backlog.
guides.decide: Lead with what decision you need from this reader, then give the supporting evidence.
traps: Reporting raw finding counts without risk context.
Sending executives technical detail with no decision attached.

deep.title: What a useful vulnerability report contains
points: Engineers need affected assets, evidence, severity, a concrete fix and an owner. Executives need risk, trends, overdue critical items against policy, and the decision required.
Useful metrics: mean time to remediate by severity, SLA compliance, vulnerability age and aging backlog, recurring findings, and coverage of the asset inventory by scans.
Recurring findings that return every quarter point to a process or root-cause problem such as missing baselines, not just missing patches.
Compliance reports show control status against a standard; risk scorecards translate findings into business impact.

guides.title: Explain the importance of security operations and incident response reporting and communication
guides.core: Incident and operations reporting convert activity into accountability and improvement, using metrics that are defined precisely.
know: Timing metrics: time to detect, respond, contain and recover. State the start and end point of each before comparing numbers.
Detection quality: precision = TP/(TP+FP); false-discovery proportion = FP/(TP+FP); true-positive rate (recall) = TP/(TP+FN); false-positive rate = FP/(FP+TN).
Precision and false-discovery proportion are complements; true-positive rate and false-positive rate are not, because they use different denominators.
After-action reporting: root cause, timeline, impact, what worked, what changes, owners and dates.
guides.decide: Write the formula before the number. Ask which denominator a stakeholder means before agreeing a target.
traps: Tuning down alerts to improve a false-positive figure while missing real threats.
Comparing time metrics that use different start points.

deep.title: Declaring, escalating and handing over incidents
points: Declare an incident when confirmed or highly probable impact to confidentiality, integrity or availability meets defined severity criteria, then follow the escalation matrix.
Share details on a need-to-know basis. Legal, communications, executives and affected owners get role-appropriate information.
A shift handover covers current status, evidence handling, open tasks, pending approvals, risks and contacts.

Regulatory duties depend on sector and location. For example, GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach where feasible.

prompt.text: An anomaly-detection model was trained on a year of network traffic that already contained a slow attacker's regular beaconing. It never alerts on that beaconing. What is the MOST likely explanation?

cases.title: Triage a suspicious privileged sign-in
cases.brief: The identity provider raised an alert for the finance director's account. Use the exhibit to decide how to respond. Think about what each piece of evidence proves and what it does not.
cases.exhibit:
09:58 SUCCESS  Berlin, DE       device=LT-4471 (managed)    MFA=push   app=Outlook
10:03 SUCCESS  Berlin, DE       device=LT-4471 (managed)    MFA=token  app=SharePoint
10:19 SUCCESS  Lagos, NG        device=unknown (browser)    MFA=satisfied-by-claim  app=Exchange Online  ua=python-requests/2.31
10:21 EVENT    New inbox rule created: forward all mail containing 'invoice' to external address
10:24 EVENT    Mail items accessed: 212 items
10:30 FAIL     Berlin, DE       device=LT-4471 (managed)    reason=session revoked by user

steps.label: What best explains the 10:19 sign-in?
options: A VPN exit node used by the director
Token or session reuse from an unmanaged client, consistent with account takeover
A time-zone display error in the portal
A scheduled backup service
steps.explain: The director's managed laptop is active in Berlin, while the 10:19 sign-in comes from an unknown client with a scripted user agent and MFA satisfied by claim rather than a new prompt. That combination suggests a stolen token or session being replayed. A VPN would normally keep the device identity and client consistent. A display error would not create a new inbox rule.

steps.label: Which finding makes this MORE than an impossible-travel false alarm?
options: The sign-in succeeded
The new forwarding rule for invoice mail and the bulk mail access
The sign-in occurred in daylight hours
The director uses Outlook
steps.explain: Post-sign-in actions are the stronger evidence. A rule that forwards invoice mail externally, followed by bulk mailbox access, matches business email compromise preparation. A successful sign-in alone is ambiguous.

steps.label: Choose the best response sequence.
options: Wait for the director to confirm travel plans before acting
Revoke all sessions and tokens, reset credentials, remove the rule, preserve sign-in and mailbox audit logs, and review other actions by the session
Delete the account and recreate it
Block Nigeria at the firewall and close the case
steps.explain: The risk is active and financial, so contain now: revoke sessions and tokens, reset credentials and remove the forwarding rule. Preserve the logs for scoping and possible legal or financial recovery steps. Deleting the account destroys evidence, and a country block does not remove a stolen token or address the existing rule.

cases.summary: Impossible travel alone is a lead. Device identity, token behavior and post-sign-in actions turned it into a confirmed takeover. Contain first, preserve evidence, then scope.

cases.title: Prioritize the weekend's vulnerability findings
cases.brief: A scan produced the findings below. You can patch two items before Monday. Decide what to fix and what to do with the rest.
cases.exhibit:
F1  CVE-A  CVSS 9.8  EPSS 0.3%   KEV=no   host=intranet-wiki      [medium]  internal only
F2  CVE-B  CVSS 7.8  EPSS 87%    KEV=yes  host=vpn-gateway-01   [high]    internet-facing
F3  CVE-C  CVSS 8.1  EPSS 41%    KEV=no   host=billing-db       [critical] internal; compensating firewall rule exists
F4  CVE-D  CVSS 5.3  EPSS 0.1%   KEV=no   host=print-server      [low]     internal only

steps.label: Which finding is the first one to remediate?
options: F1 because it has the highest CVSS
F2 because it is exploited in the wild and exposed on a high-value gateway
F3 because the asset is critical
F4 because it is quickest to fix
steps.explain: F2 combines known exploitation, high exploitation likelihood and internet exposure on an access gateway. F1 has a high score but no exploitation evidence and limited exposure. F3 matters, but a compensating rule already reduces exposure.

steps.label: What should happen with F3 on the critical billing database?
options: Ignore it because a firewall rule exists
Patch it in the next maintenance window, and verify the compensating control works and is monitored until then
Mark it a false positive
Remove the database from the scan scope
steps.explain: A compensating control reduces risk but does not remove the vulnerability. Treat it as a temporary measure: confirm it actually blocks the path, monitor, and schedule the fix. Removing it from scope hides risk.

steps.label: How should F4 be handled?
options: Immediately patch outside change control
Schedule within normal patch cycles and document the prioritization decision
Raise it to critical because every vulnerability matters
Suppress it permanently with no review date
steps.explain: Low exploitation likelihood, low severity and a low-value internal asset justify routine handling. Record why it is lower priority, and review it if exploitation evidence changes.

cases.summary: Rank by exploitation evidence and exposure on valuable assets, then severity. Compensating controls buy time; they do not close the finding.

cases.title: Report on a phishing incident
cases.brief: The incident is closed. Prepare the reporting and decide which numbers are meaningful. Use the exhibit.
cases.exhibit:
Phishing campaign start: 08:10
First user report: 08:42
SOC confirms malicious: 09:05
Mailboxes purged / indicators blocked: 09:40
Credential reset for 4 clickers: 10:15
All services normal: 11:30
Alerts from the email gateway that week: 100 (TP 30, FP 70)
Known missed phishing emails reported by users that week: 10

steps.label: Time to detect, measured from campaign start to SOC confirmation, is:
options: 32 minutes
55 minutes
90 minutes
3 hours 20 minutes
steps.explain: 09:05 minus 08:10 is 55 minutes. 32 minutes is the gap to the first user report. 90 minutes is start to purge/blocking. 3 hours 20 minutes is start to normal operations. State definitions in the report.

steps.label: What are the gateway's precision and true-positive rate for the week (using the 10 missed emails as FN)?
options: Precision 30%, true-positive rate 75%
Precision 70%, true-positive rate 30%
Precision 75%, true-positive rate 30%
Precision 30%, true-positive rate 30%
steps.explain: Precision = 30/(30+70) = 30%. True-positive rate = 30/(30+10) = 75%. The gateway catches most known phishing but produces a lot of noise.

steps.label: Which recommendation belongs in the after-action report?
options: Disable the gateway because 70% of alerts are false
Tune gateway rules to improve precision while tracking missed-phishing reports so detection coverage does not fall, and add a user-report workflow metric
Report only the total alert count to executives
Remove the incident from reporting because it was contained quickly
steps.explain: Reducing noise matters, but not at the expense of recall. Track both precision and missed detections. A useful report states root cause, timeline, impact, what worked, actions, owners and dates. Disabling the gateway removes detection; reporting only totals hides quality.

cases.summary: Define each timing metric, write the formula before the number, and tie metrics to decisions: tune for precision without losing recall.
